## Statement

No application of simulation-based inference to bridge disconnected evidence through a mechanistic or pharmacometric model exists, so the entry stands open; the generic method is mature and surveyed (arXiv:1911.01429), and the non-simulation-based version of the idea is already routine in evidence synthesis as model-based meta-analysis and dose-response NMA, where a parametric dose-response curve connects arms that are not directly compared (MBNMAdose). Simulation-based inference approximates posterior, likelihood or likelihood-ratio quantities within a specified simulator; it does not itself identify a bridge, so it can support one only where mechanistic assumptions and data already define it. The misspecification claim needs care: a misspecified simulator does not return a well-calibrated posterior, it returns a posterior calibrated only relative to the wrong model, and the approximation can add miscalibration of its own.

## Why it is open

The inferential guarantee is inherited from the simulator, so a mechanistic model that is wrong produces a bridge that carries the error without signaling it. Calibration of the inference procedure itself is computationally expensive and rarely performed, so in practice neither the model nor the approximation is checked. The result is a bridge whose apparent precision is a property of the simulator, the prior and the approximation rather than of the evidence.

## What has been tried

::: {.table-scroll}

| Work | What it contributes |
|---|---|
| [Cranmer, Brehmer & Louppe, The frontier of simulation-based inference (2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.01429) | Survey of the generic machinery, including the dependence of every guarantee on the assumed simulator and the cost of calibrating the inference procedure. |
| [MBNMAdose (R package)](https://cran.r-project.org/package=MBNMAdose) | The near neighbor the source omitted: dose-response network meta-analysis in which a parametric curve connects arms that are not directly compared, doing the same bridging job with a tractable likelihood. |

:::

## Probable solution or research direction

Develop simulation-based inference for pharmacometric and disease-process bridges across disconnected evidence, benchmarked against the dose-response and model-based network meta-analysis approaches that already perform the same bridging job with tractable likelihoods. Make simulator-misspecification checks and explicit calibration of the approximation mandatory, and report the bridge's sensitivity to the mechanistic assumptions alongside the estimate so the inherited error is visible.

## Verification

::: {.verification-trail}
**Verdict.** Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.

**The source said.** "Simulation-based inference is proposed to approximate intractable likelihoods in mechanistic or pharmacometric models, so that disease-process or exposure-response models can act as bridges between disconnected pieces of evidence. The report labels it emerging."

**What was wrong with it.** The source said a misspecified simulator returns a well-calibrated posterior for the wrong model; GPT-5.6 Sol corrected this, since calibration holds only relative to the assumed simulator and the approximation adds error of its own. The literature auditor also named the near neighbor the source omitted, dose-response and model-based network meta-analysis, which already bridges arms that are not directly compared.

Literature and prior-art check
:   **open / supported.** I found no application of simulation-based inference to bridge disconnected evidence via a mechanistic or pharmacometric model, so the entry stands open. The generic method is mature and well surveyed (Cranmer, Brehmer & Louppe, 'The frontier of simulation-based inference', arXiv:1911.01429), and the adjacent, non-SBI version of the idea already exists in evidence synthesis as model-based meta-analysis and dose-response NMA (MBNMAdose), where a parametric dose-response curve connects arms that are not directly compared; the entry does not mention this near neighbour. The two limitation claims are correct and standard in the SBI literature: the posterior is only as good as the simulator, so a misspecified mechanistic model yields a well-calibrated posterior for the wrong model, and calibration checks of the inference procedure itself are computationally expensive and often skipped. Confidence is moderate because I read surveys and abstracts, not full texts.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens
:   **open / overstated.** C1, C3, C4, and C5 are correct in qualified form. SBI approximates posterior, likelihood, or likelihood-ratio quantities within a specified simulator; it does not itself identify a bridge between disconnected evidence. C2 therefore holds only when mechanistic assumptions and data already define that bridge. Simulator misspecification does not imply that SBI returns a well-calibrated posterior: even an algorithm validated under the simulator is calibrated only relative to that model, while approximation error can introduce additional miscalibration. Posterior precision depends on the observations, simulator, prior, and approximation, not on the simulator alone. Calibration cost is method- and scale-dependent. The PAIC adaptation remains open but is an optional computational roadmap item unless an analysis actually relies on such a mechanistic bridge.

Grok 4.5, recency lens
:   **open / supported.** No cited prior_work. Simulation-based / likelihood-free inference is mature in machine learning and physics, and mechanistic/pharmacometric models are standard in model-informed drug development, but search did not find an evaluated SBI pipeline that bridges disconnected trial evidence for ITC/PAIC with mandatory simulator-misspecification checks and calibration reporting tied to a transported effect. C1 is true of SBI in general (capability, not a solved ITC problem). C2 remains a proposal. C3–C4 correctly restate well-known SBI failure modes (misspecified simulator yields calibrated wrong-model posteriors; calibration is expensive and often skipped). C5 is a report maturity label. A proposal-without-ITC-evaluation does not close the problem. Queries: simulation-based inference + (pharmacometric|disease model|meta-analysis|indirect treatment|evidence bridge); likelihood-free MIDD NMA 2023–2026; arXiv stat.ME SBI bridging trials.

Decision path
:   `R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex`

:::
